newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia dlr ends sombre week on upbeat note.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia dlr ends sombre week on upbeat note.

text.p: The Australian dollar finished a downbeat week on a minor upbeat note as the resilience of support defeated repeated attempts to extend the correction.

The day's range was only 30 basis points but within that the price action was choppy as sizeable sell orders from Japanese and Chinese banks eddied with buying linked to a samurai issue and direct from local corporates.

The bulls were carrying the day at the close but had yet to pierce offers at US$0.7920, which had capped the currency since its fall from atop 80 cents last week, and without such a break the dollar would remain vulnerable to a relapse to US$0.7810.
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the dollar was making threatening gestures at US$0.7915/20 having advanced from Thursday's late US$0.7890/95 level despite repeated setbacks.
That was still short of its US$0.7962/67 finish Friday last week, but comfortably above the US$0.7860 week low.

Traders said the firmer tone was largely a result of buying for a 20 billion yen dual currency samurai bond for Denmark, which came on top of a similar sized issue for NSW Treasury on Thursday. That helped the dollar inch up to 86.82/92 yen from 86.33/43 late Thursday, but remained well down on last Friday's 87.63/73 close.
The samurai bonds were welcomed by dollar bulls who have been concerned by a sharp slowdown in the pace of issues.

The sudden reticence of Japanese investors was thought to be partly due to the proximity of the half year end there and partly to concerns the U.S. would soon be raising rates while Australia eased, thus eating into the dollar's yield premium.

The U.S. Federal Reserve meets next Tuesday to decide on policy and most analysts here are tipping a 0.25 point hike in the 5.25 point funds rate, although they expected the vote to be a very close one. In contrast, most think the Reserve Bank will cut domestic rates by 0.5 point to 6.5 percent by year end.

Such a scenario would narrow the Australian dollar's yield premium on two and three year bonds -- the typical time scale for dual currency samurais -- to virtually nothing and make US$ samurais much more attractive to Japanese investors.

The local currency derived indirect support from a firmer US$/yen which rallied on the back of strong U.S. housing data and rises in the price components of the Philadelphia Fed survey of business conditions.
However, such signs of upbeat U.S. growth have conflicting implications for the local unit since it makes it a little more likely the Fed will hike rates at its policy meeting next week.

But strong U.S. growth was bullish for the AUD in the longer run since it promised to underpin recoveries in Japan and Europe and eventually produce the sort of synchronised world upturn which would boost the demand for, and price of, commodities.
The dollar tends to track commodity price trends over time as commodities make up over 60 percent of Australia's exports and the currency is seen as a commodity play by many investors.

All this has convinced some analysts the local dollar could weaken toward 77 cents by year end if the Fed hikes and the RBA eases as feared, but should rebound to 80 cents in 1997 as stronger world growth drives commodity prices higher.

On the technical front a week of tight consolidation had left the currency with a slight upward bias, although analysts emphasised it would have to clear US$0.7950 resistance to restore some semblance of credibility to the uptrend so badly tarnished by last week's 3/4 cent dive.
In trade weighted terms it edged ahead to 58.2 from 58.0 late Thursday.

There were no domestic data today and little next week to provide direction, but the new RBA governor Ian Macfarlance was speaking at an economists conference on Wednesday and anything he said would be closely analysed. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 373 1800
